rubric: DISCRETE MATHEMATICS / GRAPHS AND PROBABILITY / CHAPTER 9

slides.title: Graph traversals and trees
slides.main: A traversal means visiting all reachable vertices and not looping.

captions: Graph traversals and trees
While you sleep, the garbage collector, a crawler and a package manager walk their graphs
A traversal means visiting all the vertices without getting lost and without looping
Today: two ways of traversing, trees and the bridges of Königsberg
You will meet all of this in production — already recognizing it by sight

body.text: While you sleep, graphs are walked by the garbage collector, a crawler and a package manager — you will meet all of this in production, recognizing it by sight.

slides.title: The problem statement
slides.sub: A graph and a starting vertex are given
slides.main: Every reachable vertex exactly once; memory saves us from cycles.

captions: Let's state the problem honestly
Given a graph and a starting vertex: visit everything reachable — each vertex exactly once
The catch is in cycles: without memory a traversal circles forever around one ring
Any traversal has two organs: a way of choosing the next vertex and a set of visited ones
The choice gives birth to different algorithms, while the visited set is mandatory in each of them

frames.text: ×  — unreachable: the traversal never touches it

slides.title: Depth-first traversal
slides.sub: DFS: a route through a maze with a thread
slides.main: Go forward while you can; hit a dead end — step back and try another door.

captions: The first way is depth-first traversal
The rule: go forward while you can; hit a dead end — step back and try another door
A route through a maze with a thread tied to your finger: the thread remembers where we came from, and we return along it
Naturally held by a stack: put a new node on, take a dead end off, the top of the stack tells where we are

frames.text: order: A, B, D, E, G, C, F
thread: A → B → D, dead end, back to B

body.text: A dead end — we take the vertex off the stack and try another door. The thread in the maze is the stack: it remembers where you came from.

slides.title: Recursion is a stack
slides.sub: A ready-made stack built into the language for free
slides.main: Any recursive function strolling through a nested structure is a depth-first traversal.

captions: The beauty of depth-first traversal: recursion is a ready-made stack built into the language for free
The function marks a node as visited and calls itself for each unvisited neighbor; the call stack remembers the way back
This is how the DOM tree is walked: recursively descending to the children at each node
This is how directories are walked: a folder is a recursive call, a file is a leaf
Any recursive function strolling through a nested structure is a depth-first traversal, whatever you call it

frames.text: even if you never called it that

body.text: The call stack itself remembers the way back — even if you never called it depth-first traversal.

slides.title: Breadth-first traversal
slides.sub: BFS: first all the near ones, then the far ones
slides.main: The wave spreads in circles like on water; a queue instead of a stack.

captions: The second way is breadth-first traversal: first all the near ones, then the far ones
From the start we visit all the neighbors, then the neighbors of the neighbors — the wave spreads in circles like on water
To keep the wave in order, a queue is needed: "first in, first out" keeps the order by distance
The stack and the queue are the only difference in the code, while the behavior of the algorithms is radically different

frames.text: taken out on the left, added on the right

body.text: First in, first out: this order guarantees processing by circles of distance. The stack and the queue are the only difference in the code, while the behavior of the algorithms changes radically.

slides.title: Shortest paths by a wave
slides.main: In an unweighted graph breadth-first traversal finds shortest paths.

captions: Replacing the stack with a queue gives a valuable property: breadth-first traversal finds shortest paths in an unweighted graph
The wave reaches every vertex by the minimal number of edges: first distance 1, then 2
The logic of "friends of friends": social networks suggest people exactly 2–3 handshakes away
In a maze breadth leads out by the shortest route, while depth leads by the first corridor that comes along

frames.text: number = fewest edges from the start

body.text: Depth, on the other hand, can drag you along a long but first-found corridor.

slides.title: Connected components
slides.main: Each launch of a traversal drains exactly one component; the number of launches is the number of islands.

captions: A utilitarian classic: finding connected components
Walk through all the vertices; when you meet an unvisited one, launch a traversal from it and mark all its kin
Each launch drains exactly one component; the number of launches equals the number of islands
This is how isolated groups of users, clusters of services and disconnected pieces of a dependency graph are counted
Depth and breadth are interchangeable here — only the fact of complete draining matters

frames.text: for v in V: if v is not visited → traverse(v)
groups of users · clusters · pieces of dependencies
DFS or BFS — the result is the same

body.text: Depth and breadth are interchangeable here — only the fact of complete draining matters.

slides.title: A tree and the formula n − 1
slides.short: A tree and the formula n − 1
slides.main: Between any two vertices there is exactly one path — getting lost is impossible.

captions: A special place of honor on this field belongs to trees
A tree is a connected graph without cycles: between any vertices there is exactly one path, getting lost is impossible
The formula: a tree with n vertices has exactly n − 1 edges
Check: one vertex — zero edges, three vertices in a chain — two edges
Works in both directions: a connected graph with n − 1 edges is a tree; add an edge — a cycle, remove one — it falls apart

frames.text: D → B → A → C → F — the only path
+ edge D–E → cycle B–D–E; without an edge — falls apart

body.text: Check: one vertex — zero edges, three in a chain — two edges. The formula works in both directions: add an edge and a cycle is born, remove one and it falls apart into pieces.

slides.title: Trees around us
slides.sub: The most common form of graph in development
slides.main: The ideal environment for recursion: the base on the leaves, the step on the children.

captions: Trees are the most common form of graph in everyday development
A file system: a root, folders and files inside, each with exactly one parent
An abstract syntax tree: the compiler parses a program into a tree of expressions
The browser's DOM tree: markup turns into a tree of nodes
A company hierarchy and product categories are arranged the same way
It is no accident that all the recursion of the previous chapter was practiced on trees: the base on the leaves, the step on the children

body.text: It is no accident that almost all the recursion of the previous chapters was practiced precisely on trees.

slides.title: The spanning tree
slides.sub: Squeezing a skeleton out of a graph
slides.main: Keep exactly n − 1 edges so that connectivity is preserved.

captions: From the tree grows a practical problem: the spanning tree
A connected graph: keep n − 1 edges so that connectivity is preserved — a skeleton of the network with no extra edges and cycles
If the edges have prices — the minimum spanning tree: the cheapest way to connect everyone
Laying cables between servers, joining offices, clustering points on a map
The essence: squeeze a tree out of a graph

body.text: Laying cables between servers, joining offices into a network, clustering points on a map.

slides.title: The bridges of Königsberg
slides.sub: The oldest problem of graph theory
slides.main: An Eulerian path exists only if there are zero or two odd vertices.

captions: The oldest problem of graph theory, born of a walk
In Königsberg there are seven bridges across the river: can you cross each exactly once?
Euler: each visit to a vertex uses up two edges — entering and leaving, so odd degrees are possible only at the start and the finish
An Eulerian path exists only if there are zero (a closed route) or two odd vertices
In Königsberg there are four odd vertices — the walk is impossible, and graph theory was born

body.text: Each visit to a vertex uses up two edges — entering and leaving, so odd degrees can belong only to the start and the finish. The walk turned out to be impossible, and graph theory was born.

slides.title: Traversals in production
slides.sub: One pair of algorithms, many scenery changes
slides.main: The garbage collector, the dependency resolver and the crawler are DFS and BFS with a change of scenery.

captions: Let's put the traversals back into production
The garbage collector walks the graph of objects from the roots: reachable is alive, the rest is garbage
The dependency resolver walks the graph depth-first and watches a node's "gray" state to catch a cycle
A crawler is a breadth-first traversal with a set of visited addresses, limited by depth and by politeness to servers
Reachability checks in permissions, the shortest path in a game, walking the DOM in tests — the same pair of algorithms

frames.text: c → a: a is already "gray" ⇒ a cycle!
the shortest path in a game
DFS + BFS — only the scenery changes

body.text: The shortest path in a game and walking the DOM tree in tests — one and the same pair of algorithms.

slides.title: Summary
slides.main: The visited set protects against cycles, repeated launches drain the components.

captions: Summing up the chapter
Depth goes to the limit with a stack and is written with recursion; breadth spreads like a wave with a queue and gives shortest paths
The visited set protects against cycles, repeated launches drain the connected components
A tree is a connected graph without cycles, n − 1 edges: a file system, an AST, the DOM
Spanning trees are the skeleton of a network; the bridges of Königsberg taught us to tell traversable graphs by their odd degrees
Next — probability: how Bayes' theorem rules spam filters

body.text: The next, final chapter is uncertainty: probability and Bayes, who rules spam filters.
